text.p: Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) welcomed a report on its pricing by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) on Friday which calls for a one-off 25 percent cut in revenues this year, more lenient than its regulator had proposed.
But the regional electricity company (Rec), which called for the MMC review last year after clashing with regulator Ofreg over its pricing plans, warned the regulator not to push things further.

"The MMC agreed with much of NIE's case and rejected (Ofreg's) proposals. It is not now open to (Ofreg) to reject the MMC's conclusions and we shall resist any attempt on his part to do so," NIE said in a statement.

Ofreg earlier published the MMC report and said it intended to "largely accept" its proposals, which said revenues allowed by price formulas should be cut by 25 percent for 1997/98 and by two percent below inflation (RPI) annually for the following four years.
NIE had called for a one-off cut of 22 percent followed by RPI less three percent while Ofreg had targeted a 31 percent cut and then price caps of two percent below RPI for the following years.
But Ofreg head Douglas McIldoon said in a statement that he was "not...currently minded" to accept MMC recommendations on transmission and distribution "without adjustment".
The MMC said that on the basis of its assessments, NIE should see revenues of 575 million pounds ($933 million) from its transmission and distribution business at 1996/97 prices.
McIldoon said he would allow the MMC's proposals for the next two years but wanted NIE to submit further documentation before deciding on the years beyond.

He claimed Ofreg's ideas on modifications to the MMC's recommendations would mean revenues of 555 million pounds, or cuts of 15 percent in domestic bills next year, compared with 14 percent decreases under the MMC's guidelines.

NIE chief executive Patrick Haren slammed Ofreg's "clear desire to challenge the process still further," which "prolongs uncertainty and creates the risk that the regulatory framework will fall into disrepute."
Haren described Ofreg's original proposals as "garbage" when NIE took the matter to the MMC in August 1996.
"Ofreg has tried to leave it open, it's not all signed, sealed and put to bed. But I'm not sure where another appeal could go," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
NIE's shares had climbed 9.5 pence to 389.5 pence by 1020 GMT as the market reacted positively to the review's conclusions.
"It's better than Ofreg originally proposed but NIE might be disappointed the full report hasn't been accepted," the analyst said.
The initial one-off cut of 25 percent will hit profits at NIE but analysts said there should still be room for dividend growth.
They added that NIE would have to look at cutting costs and expectations are that the company will outline ways of reducing expenditure soon.
One possibility which has been rumoured is that NIE might outsource its billing operations, possibly to Vertex, the company set up by United Utilities, formed when North West Water took over Norweb.
NIE cut prices for domestic customers by at least eight percent effective April 1 in anticipation of its pricing review.

The company, which turned in pretax profits of 107.4 million pounds, up 24 percent, in the year to March 1996, blames high oil prices and generating charges along with its large geographical area and sparse population for its hefty consumer charges.
Bills in Northern Ireland have traditionally been about 20 percent higher than in England and Wales. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
